meaning: The gradient grows layer after layer (or time step after time step) because each factor is above 1, so updates become huge: loss spikes, inf or NaN.
What each layer multiplies the backward signal by: roughly weight scale × activation slope. Thirty factors of 0.9 leave 4%; thirty of 1.1 give 17×.
If the global gradient norm ‖g‖ exceeds a threshold c, rescale g to length c. Keeps the direction, caps the step. Common LLM default: 1.0.
Clamp every gradient entry into [−c, c]. Simpler than norm clipping but it changes the direction of the update.
The square root of the sum of all squared gradient entries across all parameters: how long the whole update arrow is. Worth logging every step.
Deeper plain networks reaching higher training error than shallower ones (56 vs 20 layers on CIFAR-10): an optimization failure, not overfitting. Residual connections fixed it.
A block computes y = x + F(x): the input skips around the layers and is added back. Backward, each block multiplies the gradient by 1 + F′, so there is always a factor-1 path.
The gated predecessor of ResNets (2015): y = H(x)·T(x) + x·(1 − T(x)), with a learned transform gate T deciding how much input to carry.
In a transformer, the running vector that flows through every layer via residual connections; each attention and MLP block reads from it and adds a small update.

Normalizes each feature using the mean and variance of the current mini-batch, then applies learned γ, β. Allows higher learning rates, but depends on batch-mates and needs running statistics for eval.
BatchNorm's moving averages of each feature's mean and variance, updated during training (momentum 0.1 in PyTorch) and used instead of batch statistics after model.eval().

Ioffe and Szegedy's 2015 name for the change in each layer's input distribution as earlier layers train; their explanation for BatchNorm. Later work argued the real benefit is a smoother loss landscape.
Normalizes each example (each token) over its own features. Same at training and test time, works at batch size 1: the transformer default.
LayerNorm without the mean: divide each token by the root mean square of its features, times γ. Cheaper with comparable quality; used in LLaMA-style models.
Normalizes each image over groups of channels (and all pixels). Batch-independent, so it works with 1 or 2 images per GPU in detection and segmentation.
The model fits noise in the training data: training accuracy high, validation accuracy much lower (a train/val gap), validation loss rising while training loss falls.
During training, zero each unit with probability p and scale survivors by 1/(1 − p) (inverted dropout); at test time use all units. Approximates an ensemble of 2ⁿ thinned networks.
Shrinks every weight a little toward 0 each step (equivalent to an L2 penalty for SGD). With Adam use the decoupled version, AdamW; LLMs commonly use 0.1.
Track validation loss, keep the best checkpoint, and stop when it hasn't improved for a set patience. Nearly free regularization.
Test error that rises and then falls again as models (or training time) grow past the point where they can just fit the training data (Nakkiran et al., 2019).
A network that has memorized its training set suddenly starts to generalize much later in training (Power et al., 2022, on small algorithmic tasks).
Random, label-preserving transformations of training inputs (crops, flips, color, rotation, noise) that teach invariances without new labels.
mixup blends two images and their labels with weight λ; CutMix pastes a patch of one image into another and mixes labels by area.
Automatic augmentation policies: RandAugment applies N random ops at magnitude M (2 knobs); TrivialAugment applies one random op at a random strength (no knobs).
Average a trained model's predictions over several augmented copies of each test input (AlexNet used 10 crops). Small accuracy gain, N× inference cost.
A debugging test: train on a single tiny batch; a working pipeline drives the loss to about 0. If it can't, the code is broken.
Before training, a K-class classifier should score about ln(K) (0.693 for 2, 2.303 for 10, 6.908 for 1,000). Far above means bad init; far below suggests leakage.
Information about the answer sneaking into the inputs or across data splits (duplicates, post-hoc features), producing too-good validation curves and a model that fails in practice.
Train briefly while the learning rate grows exponentially and plot loss against it; pick a value about 10× below where the loss is lowest (Smith, 2015).
